I’ve always been a big guy—working on the water your whole life, you don’t worry much about weight. But for the past year, I can’t stop looking at myself in mirrors, at windows, at any shiny surface. It’s my face—my nose, mostly. It doesn’t look right. I know people say it’s fine, but I see it: it’s crooked, too large, ruined. I check it all the time, adjust my hat, tilt my head. I’ve even started wearing sunglasses indoors so I don’t have to see it.  

I used to eat heartily—need to, on long hauls—but now, meals feel like a threat. I skip breakfast and lunch not because I’m trying to lose weight—though I have, unintentionally—but because I feel so disgusted with how I look. If I gain even a pound, it throws me into a panic, but it’s not the weight itself, it’s what it might do to my face, my appearance.  

My wife says I’m paranoid, the doctor said I’m underweight, but they don’t understand. This isn’t about being thin. It’s that my body—my face—feels like a mask I can’t remove. I know it sounds extreme, but I can’t stop watching, adjusting, avoiding how I look.
